Standard computer monitors flicker at 60 Hz — meaning they refresh 60 times per second. This creates two serious issues: • The flickering feels harsh and uncomfortable — users get headaches, eye strain, and fatigue very quickly . • The brain signals produced are weak and noisy — making it hard for the computer to accurately detect what the user intended . • You can only use frequencies that are exact divisors of 60 — so 25 Hz, 18 Hz etc. come out distorted . 2. What Was Being Used Before? Researchers tried three main approaches before this: LEDs — Very precise and bright flickering. Brain signals were clean. But LEDs can only show simple flashing lights — no text, no colors, no patterns. Standard LCD Monitors — Could show text, colors, complex visuals. But refresh rate was limited to 60, 120, or 240 Hz. The flickering was harsh. Signal quality was poor. Users got tired fast. High Refresh Rate Gaming Monitors (360 Hz) — A step up from standard LCDs. Better signal quality. But still constrained by the same fundamental limitation — the entire screen shares one backlight. You cannot control different areas independently. So every approach had a fatal flaw — nobody had figured out how to get LED - level precision with LCD - level flexibility at the same time. 3. What This Paper Proposes — The New Solution The researchers built something called PB - SSVEP — Partition Backlight SSVEP. The core idea : What if we split the backlight of an LCD screen into hundreds of small independent zones — each zone controlled separately like its own mini LED? That is exactly what they did. They took a 27 - inch display and divided its backlight into 384 independent partitions — each one powered by Mini - LEDs and controlled individually. Now each zone can flicker at its own frequency and phase — completely independently from every other zone. The LCD panel sits on top and adds the visual layer — text, colors, shapes — just like a normal screen. The result is a display that behaves like hundreds of individual LED stimulators built inside one single screen. And they pushed the refresh rate to 780 Hz — more than 13 times faster than a standard 60 Hz monitor — giving them clean, accurate, sine - wave shaped flickering at virtually any frequency they want. 4. Standard LCDs restrict stimulation frequency to f = R/N (R = refresh rate, N = integer). At 780 Hz, the system can accurately represent a much wider and finer range of stimulation frequencies (8 – 30 Hz tested, near - 100% accuracy), avoiding the distortion se en in standard 60/120/240 Hz displays. Sinusoidal stimulation more closely mimics natural neural oscillation patterns, reducing visual discomfort while maintaining strong SSVEP responses. Square waves produce harmonic distortions that can interfere with EEG signal clarity. The SPWM technique in PB - SSVEP generates near - perfect sine waves, which is a core advantage over LCD flickering. Q 6 : How do you ensure the Mini - LED backlight doesn't cause inter - partition light leakage affecting stimulus purity? The 384 - partition design with independent LED control minimizes cross - partition interference. The LCD panel further isolates visual regions. However, this is a valid engineering concern that future hardware iterations should quantify more precisely. Q 7 : What happens to BCI performance when multiple targets flicker simultaneously? Is there cross - frequency interference? The 9 - target 3×3 grid experiment ran all targets simultaneously at different frequencies (14 – 26 Hz range). The CCA algorithm separates frequency components effectively. However, at very close frequency spacing, some interference risk exists — this is an op en area for further study. One Additional Important Finding — Color and Brightness Matter The researchers didn't stop at just comparing old vs new. They also investigated how to get the best out of PB - SSVEP. Color of the stimulus target: • White works best at low frequencies (around 9 Hz) and high frequencies (30 Hz) • Green works best in the mid - frequency range (16 – 18 Hz) • Blue performed the weakest overall Brightness of the stimulus: • Medium brightness is optimal for low - frequency stimuli • Maximum brightness is better for high - frequency stimuli • This is useful practically — you don't need to run LEDs at full power all the time, saving energy and reducing glare Technical Questions Q1: What makes PB - SSVEP better than conventional LCD - SSVEP? PB - SSVEP uses a 780 Hz refresh rate Mini - LED backlight with sinusoidal pulse width modulation (SPWM), producing waveforms far closer to an ideal sine wave. This yields a 0.92 μV higher signal amplitude and 3.13 dB better SNR compared to LCD - SSVEP. Q2: Why 780 Hz refresh rate specifically? Standard LCDs restrict stimulation frequency to f = R/N (R = refresh rate, N = integer). At 780 Hz, the system can accurately represent a much wider and finer range of stimulation frequencies (8 – 30 Hz tested, near - 100% accuracy), avoiding the distortion se en in standard 60/120/240 Hz displays. Q3: How does the partition backlight work? The display has two layers — a 32×12 Mini - LED backlight array (384 partitions) and an LCD panel. Each partition's LED brightness is independently controlled via SPWM to generate the desired flickering stimulus, while the LCD overlays the visual content (te xt/color). Q4: What signal processing methods were used? Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) for frequency recognition, and Fourier transform for EEG power analysis ( α and θ waves to measure fatigue). Q 5 : Why sinusoidal coding specifically? Why not square wave or other waveforms? Sinusoidal stimulation more closely mimics natural neural oscillation patterns, reducing visual discomfort while maintaining strong SSVEP responses. Square waves produce harmonic distortions that can interfere with EEG signal clarity. The SPWM technique in PB - SSVEP generates near - perfect sine waves, which is a core advantage over LCD flickering. Q 6 : How do you ensure the Mini - LED backlight doesn't cause inter - partition light leakage affecting stimulus purity? The 384 - partition design with independent LED control minimizes cross - partition interference. The LCD panel further isolates visual regions. However, this is a valid engineering concern that future hardware iterations should quantify more precisely. Q 7 : What happens to BCI performance when multiple targets flicker simultaneously? Is there cross - frequency interference? The 9 - target 3×3 grid experiment ran all targets simultaneously at different frequencies (14 – 26 Hz range). The CCA algorithm separates frequency components effectively. However, at very close frequency spacing, some interference risk exists — this is an op en area for further study. Q 8 : Why were only 8 – 30 Hz frequencies tested? What about the high frequency band above 30 Hz? The study focused on practically relevant low - to - mid frequency ranges where SSVEP responses are strongest. High - frequency stimuli (>30 Hz) are imperceptible to humans consciously, reducing fatigue risk, but also producing weaker cortical responses. PB - SSVE P's 780 Hz refresh rate technically supports high - frequency stimulation — this is a promising direction for future work. Q 9 : How stable is the Wi - Fi synchronization between the stimulus program and EEG recorder? The system achieves less than 1 ms synchronization precision via a dedicated 5 GHz WiFi module with a synchronization center. The stimulus and data reception programs run independently on the workstation communicating via TCP/IP to prevent data loss. Q 1 0 : Could temperature variation of Mini - LEDs over time affect stimulus fidelity during long sessions? This is a thoughtful hardware concern not explicitly addressed in the paper. LED thermal drift could theoretically affect brightness consistency in prolonged use — a gap worth acknowledging and flagging for future standardization testing under BIS framewor ks. Both PB - SSVEP and LCD - SSVEP used the same physical display (27 - inch, 3840×2160), switching between modes — eliminating hardware differences as a confound. The authors acknowledge this openly. Neuroscience & EEG Signal Questions Q 19 : Why were only occipital/parietal electrodes used? Could more electrodes improve accuracy? SSVEP signals originate from the visual cortex located in the occipital - parietal region. The 8 electrodes (PO5, PO3, POz, PO4, PO6, O1, Oz, O2) optimally cover this region. Adding more electrodes increases setup complexity without proportional accuracy gai ns for SSVEP - specific tasks. Q2 0 : How do you handle EEG artifacts from eye blinks and muscle movements? Raw EEG was filtered using 49 – 51 Hz notch filtering to remove power frequency interference, followed by 1 – 60 Hz bandpass filtering, and linear regression to remove eye electrical noise. Subjects were also instructed to minimize movements during critical re cording periods. Q2 1 : Is CCA sufficient for real - time BCI applications or do you need deep learning? CCA is computationally lightweight and well - suited for real - time applications with low latency. Deep learning approaches can improve accuracy further but demand more processing power and training data. For practical deployment especially in resource - limite d settings, CCA remains highly viable. Hybrid CCA - deep learning is an active research direction. Q2 2 : How does the system perform for users with epilepsy risk? Is flickering safe? This is a critical safety question. The paper acknowledges that low and mid - frequency flickering can trigger seizures in susceptible individuals. PB - SSVEP's sinusoidal modulation is gentler than hard on - off flickering, reducing seizure risk. However, indiv iduals with photosensitive epilepsy should be excluded — this needs clear safety guidelines, potentially a BIS standard. Q2 3 : What is the minimum training time needed for a new user to operate this BCI? The current paradigm requires no explicit user training since SSVEP responses are involuntary — users simply gaze at the target. However, adaptation time for electrode fitting and task familiarization was built into the experimental protocol. This zero - tra ining - data advantage is a strong practical benefit. Q.
